title: The haptic perception of spatial orientations
review_question: This review examines the isotropy of the perception of spatial orientations in the haptic system.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies on haptic perception of spatial orientations, focusing on the 'oblique effect' in adults, children, and infants, and examining factors such as gravitational cues, memory constraints, reference frames, and contextual cues.

findings.antecedent: Haptic exploration of spatial orientations (e.g., rods) in a spatial plane intrinsic to the haptic system
findings.quote: This review examines the isotropy of the perception of spatial orientations in the haptic system. It shows the existence of an oblique effect.

findings.antecedent: Gravitational cues (e.g., unsupported forearm, natural gravity conditions)
findings.source: Role of gravitational cues in the haptic oblique effect
findings.quote: gravitational cues are crucial when the haptic oblique effect is present in the three planes in blindfolded participants and in the ipsilateral reproduction condition.

findings.antecedent: Exploration/reproduction in the horizontal plane (vs. frontal/sagittal) with ipsilateral hand
findings.source: Role of gravitational cues in the haptic oblique effect
findings.quote: the presence of an oblique effect in the frontal and sagittal planes and its absence in the horizontal plane.
the reproduction by the other hand of an oblique requires a complex transformation of the sensory-motor trace of the scanning movement.

findings.source: Initial hypotheses on the origin of the haptic oblique effect
findings.quote: prior visual perceptual experience and exploration-reproduction movements were responsible for the haptic oblique effect.

findings.antecedent: Increased memorization constraints (e.g., interfering verbal or motor task during delay)
findings.source: Role of previous visual experience and memory in the haptic oblique effect
findings.quote: the reduction of available attentional or cognitive resources by an interfering task caused an oblique effect in a condition in which it was not usually observed.
tilting affected vertical perception in the production task and also in orientation reproduction... the gravitational vertical and horizontal orientations no longer appear to act as reference norms.

findings.consequent: Precision of orientation perception (haptic oblique effect magnitude)
findings.quote: When the context was congruent with the standard orientations, the precision of adjustments was significantly improved.

findings.source: Developmental aspect of the oblique effects
findings.quote: an oblique effect may be present when the shoulder-arm-hand system of the infants from the age of 5 months could actively move freely in the air.
the haptic processing of orientations was clearly anisotropic. The vertical orientation was reproduced most precisely.

synthesis_conclusions: The haptic perception of spatial orientations is anisotropic, exhibiting an 'oblique effect' where vertical and horizontal orientations are perceived more accurately than oblique ones.

The haptic oblique effect is influenced by gravitational cues, the plane of exploration, the mode of reproduction (ipsilateral vs. contralateral hand), prior visual experience, and memory constraints.
The effect is defined within a subjective reference frame that integrates both egocentric (body-centered) and geocentric (gravity-based) cues.
The haptic oblique effect is considered a 'Class 2 oblique effect,' suggesting it arises from higher-level cognitive processing rather than early sensory stages.
The haptic oblique effect is present from infancy to adulthood, with developmental influences from gravitational cues.
In 3D space, haptic orientation processing remains anisotropic, with vertical orientations being most precisely reproduced, and in-plane and out-of-plane angular components processed independently.
evidence_gaps: Further studies are needed to understand the complex patterns of results observed in 3D space for haptic orientation perception.

More research is required to determine if the lack of correlation between visual and haptic oblique effect magnitudes reflects only a difference in the degree of anisotropy or different positioning of subjective axes across modalities.
The distinction between accuracy and precision in haptic oblique effect studies needs further investigation.

Existing cognitive models (e.g., Category-Adjustment, Dynamic Field Theory) need to address issues specific to the haptic modality, such as the role of gravity or the coding of orientation in 3D space.

moderators.effect: The presence and strength of gravitational cues modulate the magnitude and presence of the haptic oblique effect, with stronger cues generally leading to a more pronounced effect.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect is absent in supported forearm conditions or with reduced gravity, but present with normal gravity or unsupported forearm.

moderators.effect: The spatial plane in which orientations are explored and reproduced influences the haptic oblique effect, with the effect being present in frontal and sagittal planes but sometimes absent in the horizontal plane under ipsilateral reproduction.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect present in frontal/sagittal planes; absent in horizontal plane with ipsilateral reproduction but present with contralateral reproduction.

moderators.effect: The use of the contralateral hand for reproduction tends to induce or strengthen the oblique effect compared to ipsilateral reproduction, suggesting a more complex sensorimotor transformation.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect present in contralateral conditions, sometimes absent in ipsilateral conditions (e.g., horizontal plane, uninformed).

moderators.effect: Prior knowledge or visual experience of standard orientations can influence the magnitude of the haptic oblique effect, with informed participants showing a stronger effect.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect maximal in informed contralateral condition, diminished in uninformed contralateral.

moderators.variable: Memory constraints/Cognitive load (interfering tasks, delay duration)
moderators.effect: Increased cognitive load or memory demands (e.g., during a delay period with interfering tasks) can induce or strengthen the haptic oblique effect, even in conditions where it would otherwise be absent.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect absent with reduced gravity and unoccupied delay, but present with interfering verbal or motor tasks regardless of gravity.

moderators.effect: Tilting the body affects the perception of vertical and horizontal orientations, leading to the disappearance of the haptic oblique effect in tilted conditions, as the subjective vertical becomes the most accurately perceived orientation.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect present in upright body condition, absent in tilted body conditions.

moderators.effect: The presence of congruent haptic contextual cues can enhance the precision of orientation perception and weaken the haptic oblique effect.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Precision of adjustments significantly improved with congruent contextual cues, weakening the oblique effect.

moderators.effect: The haptic oblique effect is observed across different age groups, from infancy to adulthood, with its presence in infants being linked to the development of the shoulder-arm-hand system and gravitational cues.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Oblique effect present from 5 months of age, influenced by gravitational cues.

limitations: The studies on the haptic oblique effect have used a limited set of stimuli (vertical, horizontal, and two main diagonals), which might preclude the observation of biases toward the closest diagonal.
The analysis of constant errors in haptic oblique effect studies has not revealed systematic directional errors, which is a limitation for applying models like CA and DFT directly.
